problem: Vertically scaled single points of failure, such as relational databases in its own data centre, put the service at risk.
title: Netflix moves from its own data centres to AWS after a database failure
context: In August 2008 a major database corruption stopped Netflix shipping DVDs for three days.
decision_made: Move to the cloud, choosing AWS for its scale and range of services, and rebuild systems rather than lift and shift.
action_taken: Migrated over about seven years, finishing in early 2016 when its last in-house data centre was shut; the content delivery network stayed in-house.
observed_outcome: Netflix completed the migration and said cloud costs per streaming start ended up a fraction of those in the data centre; cost saving was a side effect of the move.
lessons: A failure can justify a deep architectural change, and redesigning for the cloud matters more than moving servers.
limitations: Cost and reliability claims come from Netflix. The original tech blog post was not opened directly, and the company's later cloud bills were not checked.

claims.claim_text: Netflix began moving to the cloud after a database corruption in August 2008 kept it from shipping DVDs for three days.
Netflix completed its migration and shut its last in-house data centre in early 2016.
